claim: The Caenorhabditis elegans unc-13 gene is required for SV exocytosis.
source: The Caenorhabditis elegans unc-13 gene is required for SV exocytosis, and encodes long and short isoforms (UNC-13L and S).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about the unc-13 gene.

claim: The unc-13 gene encodes long and short isoforms (UNC-13L and S).
source: The Caenorhabditis elegans unc-13 gene is required for SV exocytosis, and encodes long and short isoforms (UNC-13L and S).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the domain structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fast release was mediated by UNC-13L.
source: Fast release was mediated by UNC-13L, whereas slow release required both UNC-13 proteins and was inhibited by Tomosyn.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data in Figures 3 and 4 showing that UNC-13L rescue produces faster EPSC kinetics and EGTA-resistant release.

claim: Slow release required both UNC-13 proteins.
source: Fast release was mediated by UNC-13L, whereas slow release required both UNC-13 proteins and was inhibited by Tomosyn.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing that unc-13[L-S+] mutants have severe defects, but UNC-13L rescue in these mutants restores both fast and slow release.

claim: Slow release was inhibited by Tomosyn.
source: Fast release was mediated by UNC-13L, whereas slow release required both UNC-13 proteins and was inhibited by Tomosyn.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6 and 7 showing that tom-1 mutants have increased slow release and that inactivating TOM-1 in unc-13[L-S+] mutants restores function.

claim: The spatial location of each protein correlated with its effect.
source: The spatial location of each protein correlated with its effect. Proteins adjacent to the dense projection mediated fast release, while those controlling slow release were more distal or diffuse.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1 showing UNC-13L is colocalized with UNC-10/RIM at active zones while UNC-13S has diffuse distribution.

claim: Proteins adjacent to the dense projection mediated fast release.
source: Proteins adjacent to the dense projection mediated fast release, while those controlling slow release were more distal or diffuse.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing UNC-13L and UNC-10/RIM localization near dense projections and their role in fast release.

claim: Proteins controlling slow release were more distal or diffuse.
source: Proteins adjacent to the dense projection mediated fast release, while those controlling slow release were more distal or diffuse.
evidence: This is supported by imaging showing UNC-13S has diffuse distribution and prior immuno-EM studies showing TOM-1 is distal to dense projections.

claim: The C2A domain binds RIM.
source: C2A, which binds RIM (a protein associated with calcium channels), anchored UNC-13 at active zones and shortened the latency of release.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature on Munc13-RIM interactions.

claim: RIM is a protein associated with calcium channels.
source: C2A, which binds RIM (a protein associated with calcium channels), anchored UNC-13 at active zones and shortened the latency of release.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The C2A domain anchored UNC-13 at active zones.
source: C2A, which binds RIM (a protein associated with calcium channels), anchored UNC-13 at active zones and shortened the latency of release.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing that C2AR has increased colocalization with UNC-10/RIM compared to R alone.

claim: The C2A domain shortened the latency of release.
source: C2A, which binds RIM (a protein associated with calcium channels), anchored UNC-13 at active zones and shortened the latency of release.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8H showing that C2AR has shorter latency than R.

claim: A calmodulin binding site accelerated release.
source: A calmodulin binding site accelerated release but had little effect on UNC-13's spatial localization.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9 showing that CaMR produces faster release kinetics than R, and this effect is eliminated by the F574R mutation.

claim: The calmodulin binding site had little effect on UNC-13's spatial localization.
source: A calmodulin binding site accelerated release but had little effect on UNC-13's spatial localization.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 9B-D showing that CaMR has diffuse distribution similar to R.

claim: UNC-13L, UNC-13S, and Tomosyn form a molecular code that dictates the timing of neurotransmitter release.
source: These results suggest that UNC-13L, UNC-13S, and Tomosyn form a molecular code that dictates the timing of neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the collective data showing differential roles of these proteins in fast and slow release.

claim: The unc-13 gene contains two promoters.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The upstream promoter drives expression of long isoforms.
source: The upstream promoter drives expression of long isoforms, while a downstream promoter (which lies in the intron between exons 13 and 14) drives expression of short isoforms (hereafter referred to as UNC-13L and UNC-13S, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the gene structure.

claim: The downstream promoter lies in the intron between exons 13 and 14.

source: UNC-13L accelerates release by two mechanisms: increasing the spatial proximity of primed SVs to calcium channels and enhancing the calcium sensitivity of release by binding to calmodulin.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by CaM-binding site analysis.

claim: TOM-1 inhibits SV priming by binding to plasma membrane SNAREs, forming inactive SNARE complexes.
source: Prior studies showed that TOM-1 inhibits SV priming, and that it does so by binding to plasma membrane SNAREs, forming inactive SNARE complexes (Gracheva et al., 2006; McEwen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Tomosyn's effect on synaptic transmission is mediated primarily by inhibiting UNC-13S-mediated release.
source: Here we show that Tomosyn's effect on synaptic transmission is mediated primarily by inhibiting UNC-13S-mediated release.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by genetic interaction data.

claim: The apparent selectivity for inhibiting slow release could result from the distal localization of the TOM-1 protein.
source: The apparent selectivity for inhibiting slow release could result from the distal localization of the TOM-1 protein, as immuno-EM studies indicate that TOM-1 staining peaks ∼300 nm from the dense projection (Gracheva et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculated based on prior immuno-EM data.

claim: TOM-1 staining peaks ∼300 nm from the dense projection.
source: The apparent selectivity for inhibiting slow release could result from the distal localization of the TOM-1 protein, as immuno-EM studies indicate that TOM-1 staining peaks ∼300 nm from the dense projection (Gracheva et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior immuno-EM studies.

claim: The synaptic abundance of UNC-13S is increased in tom-1 mutants.
source: We previously reported that the synaptic abundance of UNC-13S is increased in tom-1 mutants, perhaps because the rate of distal SV fusions had increased (McEwen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Tomosyn inhibits priming and fusion of distal SVs.
source: Taken together, these results strongly support the idea that Tomosyn inhibits priming and fusion of distal SVs.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data on TOM-1 localization and function.

claim: Each synapse contains a single dense projection that is surrounded by a pool of docked SVs.
source: Each synapse contains a single dense projection that is surrounded by a pool of docked SVs, where docking occurs over a 1-μm domain of the presynaptic plasma membrane (Weimer et al., 2006; Hammarlund et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior EM studies.

claim: Docking occurs over a 1-μm domain of the presynaptic plasma membrane.
source: Each synapse contains a single dense projection that is surrounded by a pool of docked SVs, where docking occurs over a 1-μm domain of the presynaptic plasma membrane (Weimer et al., 2006; Hammarlund et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior EM studies.

claim: A mutation inactivating both UNC-13 isoforms decreased SV docking across the entire active zone.
source: A mutation inactivating both UNC-13 isoforms decreased SV docking across the entire active zone (i.e., <350 nm from the dense projection) (Gracheva et al., 2006; Weimer et al., 2006; Hammarlund et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior EM studies.

claim: Docking of proximal SVs was significantly reduced in unc-13(e1091) [L−S+] mutants (<100 nm from dense projections).
source: By contrast, docking of proximal SVs was significantly reduced in unc-13(e1091) [L−S+] mutants (<100 nm from dense projections) and in unc-10 RIM mutants (<50 nm from dense projections), whereas docking of distal SVs was unaffected in both mutants (Weimer et al., 2006; Hammarlund et al., 2007; Gracheva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior EM studies.

claim: Docking of proximal SVs was significantly reduced in unc-10 RIM mutants (<50 nm from dense projections).
source: By contrast, docking of proximal SVs was significantly reduced in unc-13(e1091) [L−S+] mutants (<100 nm from dense projections) and in unc-10 RIM mutants (<50 nm from dense projections), whereas docking of distal SVs was unaffected in both mutants (Weimer et al., 2006; Hammarlund et al., 2007; Gracheva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior EM studies.

claim: Docking of distal SVs was unaffected in unc-13(e1091) [L−S+] and unc-10 RIM mutants.
source: By contrast, docking of proximal SVs was significantly reduced in unc-13(e1091) [L−S+] mutants (<100 nm from dense projections) and in unc-10 RIM mutants (<50 nm from dense projections), whereas docking of distal SVs was unaffected in both mutants (Weimer et al., 2006; Hammarlund et al., 2007; Gracheva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior EM studies.

claim: Corresponding patterns of docking defects were observed in mouse Munc13 and RIM knockouts.
source: Corresponding patterns of docking defects were observed in mouse Munc13 and RIM knockouts (Siksou et al., 2009; Han et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: SVs docked proximal to the dense projection are required for fast release.
source: We found that unc-13(e1091) [L−S+] and unc-10 RIM mutations made evoked release slower and more loosely coupled to calcium entry, both indicating that SVs docked proximal to the dense projection are required for fast release.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data in mutants with proximal docking defects.

claim: The proportion of docked SVs that are <100 nm from the dense projection is ∼40%.
source: Finally, the proportion of docked SVs that are <100 nm from the dense projection (15/38, or ∼40%) (Hammarlund et al., 2007) is similar to the fraction of evoked release that was EGTA resistant in our conditions.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior EM data.

claim: The proportion of docked SVs <100 nm from the dense projection is similar to the fraction of evoked release that was EGTA resistant.
source: Finally, the proportion of docked SVs that are <100 nm from the dense projection (15/38, or ∼40%) (Hammarlund et al., 2007) is similar to the fraction of evoked release that was EGTA resistant in our conditions.
evidence: This is stated comparing EM data to electrophysiology data.

claim: Fast ACh release is mediated by the subpopulation of SVs that are docked adjacent to dense projections (<100 nm).
source: Thus, electrophysiological recordings, ultrastructural analysis of SV docking, immuno-EM localization of priming proteins (UNC-10/RIM, UNC-13L, and TOM-1), and sensitivity to EGTA inhibition all support a model whereby fast ACh release is mediated by the subpopulation of SVs that are docked adjacent to dense projections (<100 nm), while slow release is mediated by fusion of distal SVs (100–350 nm from dense projections).
evidence: This is the model proposed based on the collective data.

claim: Slow release is mediated by fusion of distal SVs (100–350 nm from dense projections).
source: Thus, electrophysiological recordings, ultrastructural analysis of SV docking, immuno-EM localization of priming proteins (UNC-10/RIM, UNC-13L, and TOM-1), and sensitivity to EGTA inhibition all support a model whereby fast ACh release is mediated by the subpopulation of SVs that are docked adjacent to dense projections (<100 nm), while slow release is mediated by fusion of distal SVs (100–350 nm from dense projections).
evidence: This is the model proposed based on the collective data.

claim: The rise time of fast and slow release differ by ∼2 ms.
source: The rise time of fast and slow release differ by ∼2 ms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the kinetic data.

claim: If the difference in rise time was caused solely by a diffusional delay in calcium binding, slow SVs would have to be 3 μm farther from calcium channels than fast SVs.
source: If this difference was caused solely by a diffusional delay in calcium binding, slow SVs would have to be 3 μm farther from calcium channels than fast SVs (assuming Dca = 200 µm2/s).
evidence: This is calculated based on diffusion kinetics.

claim: Exocytosis of UNC-13S primed SVs is intrinsically slower than that of UNC-13L primed vesicles.
source: Thus, it seems likely that exocytosis of UNC-13S primed SVs is intrinsically slower than that of UNC-13L primed vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic differences that cannot be explained by spatial separation alone.

claim: The analogous calmodulin-binding site in mouse Munc13-1 and Munc13-2 is required for augmentation.
source: The analogous calmodulin-binding site in mouse Munc13-1 and Munc13-2 is required for augmentation, a form of short-term plasticity (Junge et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: It was proposed that calmodulin binding to Munc13 comprises a calcium sensor for short-term plasticity.
source: Based on these results, it was proposed that calmodulin binding to Munc13 comprises a calcium sensor for short-term plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as a prior hypothesis from the literature.

claim: The calmodulin-binding site accelerates release.
source: Our results suggest that this calmodulin-binding site also accelerates release.
evidence: This is stated based on the CaMR data.

claim: The faster kinetics of UNC-13L-mediated release results from both tighter spatial coupling to calcium channels and faster intrinsic kinetics of exocytosis.
source: Thus, the faster kinetics of UNC-13L-mediated release results from both tighter spatial coupling to calcium channels and faster intrinsic kinetics of exocytosis.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the domain analysis experiments.

claim: UNC-13L promotes but is not required for slow release.
source: Thus, UNC-13L promotes but is not required for slow release.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing UNC-13L restores slow release in unc-13[L-S+] mutants.

claim: The UNC-13L requirement for slow release was reduced when the total number of primed SVs was increased.
source: The UNC-13L requirement for slow release was reduced (but not eliminated) when the total number of primed SVs was increased (by inactivating Tomosyn or by overexpressing UNC-13S).
evidence: This is stated based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: Fast and slow release could be independently adjusted by modulatory pathways.
source: In this manner, fast and slow release could be independently adjusted by modulatory pathways.
evidence: This is speculated based on the finding that they are mediated by distinct proteins.

claim: Both forms of release can occur in isolation.
source: We were able to construct mutants in which evoked release is mediated purely by either the fast or slow mechanism. Thus, both forms of release can occur in isolation.
evidence: This is stated based on the UNC-13L and UNC-13S rescue experiments.

claim: Fast SVs are not derived from maturation of slow SVs, and vice versa.
source: These results imply that fast SVs are not derived from maturation of slow SVs, and vice versa.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fast and slow release can occur independently.

claim: Fast and slow release comprise independent exocytosis mechanisms that operate in parallel.
source: Our results are more compatible with the idea that fast and slow release comprise independent exocytosis mechanisms that operate in parallel.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data.

claim: Fast and slow release share a requirement for UNC-13L.
source: Fast and slow release share a requirement for UNC-13L, which provides a potential mechanism for coordinately regulating changes in these two release pathways.
evidence: This is stated based on the genetic data.

claim: Adjusting the contributions of fast and slow release will alter the duration of postsynaptic responses.
source: Adjusting the contributions of fast and slow release will alter the duration of postsynaptic responses.
evidence: This is speculated based on the kinetic differences.

claim: Prolonged EPSCs will result in increased integration of synaptic inputs.
source: Prolonged EPSCs will result in increased integration of synaptic inputs, which could alter the rate of postsynaptic spiking.
evidence: This is speculated based on general principles of synaptic integration.

claim: Shifting the kinetics of postsynaptic responses could alter spike timing-dependent plasticity.
source: Shifting the kinetics of postsynaptic responses could also alter spike timing-dependent plasticity.
evidence: This is speculated based on general principles of plasticity.

claim: Mutations linked to Autism alter the kinetics of neurotransmitter release.
source: Consistent with this idea, we recently showed that mutations linked to Autism alter the kinetics of neurotransmitter release (Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The kinetics of neurotransmitter release are dictated by a protein code consisting of fast (UNC-10/RIM, UNC-13L) and slow (UNC-13L, UNC-13S, and Tomosyn) priming factors.
source: In summary, we propose that the kinetics of neurotransmitter release are dictated by a protein code consisting of fast (UNC-10/RIM, UNC-13L) and slow (UNC-13L, UNC-13S, and Tomosyn) priming factors, which mediate fusion of proximal and distal SVs, respectively.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: All these molecules are conserved across phylogeny.
source: All these molecules are conserved across phylogeny, and orthologous proteins are found at both NMJs and central synapses.
evidence: This is stated based on general knowledge of protein conservation.

claim: Orthologous proteins are found at both NMJs and central synapses.
source: All these molecules are conserved across phylogeny, and orthologous proteins are found at both NMJs and central synapses.
evidence: This is stated based on general knowledge.

claim: The basic mechanisms governing the kinetics of neurotransmitter release are ancient and will apply to many synapses.
source: Thus, we propose that the basic mechanisms governing the kinetics of neurotransmitter release are ancient, and will apply to many synapses.
evidence: This is speculated based on the conservation of the proteins.

claim: Munc13 proteins that lack C2A domains (bMunc13-2 and Munc13-3) are located more distally and mediate slow release at the Calyx of Held.
source: Consistent with this idea, a recent study showed that Munc13 proteins that lack C2A domains (bMunc13-2 and Munc13-3) are located more distally and mediate slow release at the Calyx of Held (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to recent literature supporting the model.
